# WebRTC The Magic of Real-Time Communication

The video explains WebRTC, the technology that allows direct video calls in the browser. Shows the four steps of the connection, how STUN and TURN servers bypass NAT, where technology is used, its advantages and limits, and the risk of real IP leak, even with VPN.

Video by Maurício Yokoyama Issei, published on January 6, 2026 (5 min 53 s).
Watch: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lezsF_27EXI

_The video and the transcript are in Portuguese. The minutes between brackets, such as [04:12], point to the excerpt of the video._

## The magic of the call in the browser

You can make a direct video call in the browser without installing anything. It seems magical: you open a tab, click on a link and the conversation begins [00:00]. Behind is the WebRTC [00:22].

The WebRTC is like an instruction manual that every modern browser already brings. It teaches two devices to talk directly, in a fast and secure connection, to video, voice or any kind of data [00:22].

## The four-step connection

There is a well-defined process that turns two unknown browsers into conversational partners [00:42]:

1. Signaling: browsers exchange something like digital business cards, so one can find the other [01:04].
2. Connection: the hardest part, finding a free way on the internet [01:04].
3. Security: everything is encrypted [01:24].
4. Communication: the conversation begins [01:24].

## NAT and STUN and TURN servers

The villain is the NAT. Most devices are behind a router that hides the actual IP address. This is good for security, but it hinders the direct connection: it is like calling someone who only has an internal extension [01:24].

The WebRTC has two helpers [01:45]:

- The STUN server: the browser asks what is its address seen from outside, on the internet, and STUN answers [01:45].
- The TURN server, Plan B: If the direct connection fails, it receives the packages from one side and delivers from the other, like a mailman. It is slower, but ensures communication [02:07].

## Where WebRTC appears

Applications go beyond video call [02:28]: video conferencing, technical support with screen access, point-to-point file sharing and even remote control of robots and vehicles. Anything that needs instant communication probably uses WebRTC [02:49].

## Advantages and limits

The WebRTC is a two-edged knife [03:11]. The advantages [03:11]:

- It is an open pattern without one owner only [03:11].
- Encryption is mandatory [03:11].
- It has very low latency [03:32].
- Works in the browser, without plugin [03:32].

The limits [03:32]:

- Simplicity hides a lot of complexity, and climbing for many people is difficult [03:52].
- It requires a lot of computer or mobile processing [03:52].
- Even being direct, communication needs a central server for initial contact between browsers [03:52].

## The privacy dilemma

The most sensitive point: for the direct connection to work, both devices need to know each other's real IP. It is a requirement of protocol [04:15].

It's not a bug, it's the design of the protocol. But this exchange of IPs can, in some cases, pierce the protection of a VPN, and a malicious site could, in theory, discover the real IP of those who browse [04:37].

Deactivating WebRTC is not the only way out [04:59]:

- A good quality VPN usually avoids this leak [04:59].
- Browser extensions create a button to turn on and off WebRTC [05:19].
- Those who almost never make video calls in the browser can disable it in the settings, the strongest protection [05:19].

The final question: what is the right balance between instant communication and privacy? The answer is personal [05:19].

## Frequently Asked Questions

### What are STUN and TURN servers for?

STUN informs the browser of its public address on the Internet. TURN relays packages when direct connection is not possible [01:45].

### Can WebRTC leak my IP even with VPN?

In some cases, yes, because direct connection requires real IP. A VPN of quality, extension or deactivation in the browser reduces risk [04:37].

## About the video

Have you ever stopped to think how it is possible to make a direct browser video call (like in Google Meet or Zoom) without having to install any heavy programs? 

The answer is not magic, it's technology! In this video, we unveiled WebRTC (Web Real-Time Communication), the protocol that revolutionized the way we communicate on the internet.

Let us simply and visually explain how two computers connect directly, the technical challenges that take place behind the scenes (such as routers and firewalls) and the truth about the security and privacy of your data.

In this video you'll learn:  The 4-step ritual to connect two navigators.  STUN and TURN.  . Tips to protect your privacy.

If you like to understand how the internet works "under the hood", this video is for you!
